Every Telegram program connects with an API pair: an API ID and an API hash that name the application. TgWitness ships a pool of public pairs, among them the pair of Telegram Desktop published in its open source code, and uses them unless you enter your own.

Every app you sign in with is a separate session with its own authorization key. The API ID and API hash only name the application; they are not a key to another app's activity. Using the same pair as the official app, or the same pair in two programs, changes nothing.

Every bot you write to receives your user ID, name, username, language and Premium status. A “Share phone number” button sends your real number in one tap. Search bots built on leaked databases match user IDs and usernames to phone numbers, names and other accounts, and a long-lived main account is usually in them.
Every request and answer is encrypted with the session's authorization key, not with the API hash. Knowing the API hash decrypts nothing.

Telegram restricts and bans accounts it does not trust, with no violation at all, and it happens often. You can check this too. Putting your main account under that risk is a really bad idea: a ban takes its chats, contacts, the channels and groups it owns, Saved Messages and username.
